paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Sour Lake, Texas, took place on July 9, 1903, when notices ordered Black people out of the oil town and a mob raided Black labor camps that night. It followed a report that a railroad brakeman had been shot by a Black man at Nome Junction. Fifty to two hundred people were reported driven out; within days Black workers were promised protection and began to return.
A New Orleans dispatch described "considerable ill-feeling" in the Sour Lake oil field between white workers, mostly Northern and Western men, and Black workers.

On the morning of July 9 a Southern Pacific brakeman was shot at Nome. A Beaumont special to the San Antonio Daily Light named him W. D. Thompson, shot "by a negro tramp," and called the wound not necessarily fatal. The Associated Press called him Bud Thompson and reported him "fatally wounded."

Within minutes of the news reaching Sour Lake, notices went up in twenty-five or thirty places: "Nigger, don't let the sun go down on you in Sour Lake to-night." A Houston dispatch to the New York Sun said "some person" posted them after "a hasty meeting" in the oil field.

More than fifty Black residents left that day for Houston and Beaumont, many of them on foot. Armed men guarded a restaurant employing Black workers, where "an effort will be made to give the negroes protection."

That night a mob reported at five hundred men raided two Black camps, one in the "Shoe String" district of the oil field and one of Southern Pacific construction workers. The occupants fled under about one hundred shots; in the dark, no one knew whether anyone was hit. A Mexican worker in the construction gang had his head "beaten into a pulp." Hotel and restaurant owners were told to discharge all Black employees "at once"; about twenty-five Black people remained, most under guard in one restaurant.

By July 10, Houston dispatches reported the trouble quieted and that Black workers would be protected if they wished to stay, "the hoodlum element to the contrary notwithstanding." The same report said the Mexican would probably recover and that a beaten Black man had disappeared. A New Orleans dispatch of July 11 credited "the better class of white citizens" with intervening when the mob threatened law-abiding Black workers. On July 13 the San Antonio Daily Light reported that Black residents were returning and the danger of trouble was over.
No report of arrests, an inquest, or Thompson's death or recovery was found.

White papers relied mainly on the Associated Press dispatch, which ran on July 10 from Indianapolis to Salt Lake City and later in Raleigh, Atlanta and small weeklies. Many printed the notice's slur, the Indianapolis Journal in its subhead and the Deseret Evening News in its headline, "Notice to 'Niggers.'" Southern headlines anticipated wider conflict ("Race War May Be the Result," in the Montgomery Advertiser), and the Atlanta Constitution headed its story "Murder Near Sour Lake" though no paper reported Thompson dead.

New York papers framed it as an attack: "Shooting Negroes in Texas" and "Drive Negroes From Oil Fields." The Sun's follow-up, "Stood Up for the Negroes," credited leading whites with checking the mob but counted "the entire criminal and dangerous element" among the expelled. Raleigh's News and Observer put "Requested" in quotation marks in its subhead on the "Exodus of Blacks," and weekly digests reduced the affair to a line such as "Texans drive negroes from Sour Lake oil fields."

The only Black-press coverage found was in the Iowa State Bystander of July 10, which ran the wire story under the headline "Drive Negroes From Town" and the subhead "Murder of Brakeman On Southern Pacific Starts War." It ran the raid report without comment; no Black-press editorial or letter was found.

Counts of those driven out rose with time: over fifty by the evening of July 9 in the AP account, about one hundred in the Sun's Houston dispatch, and about two hundred in the New Orleans dispatch. Thompson was "fatally wounded" in the AP account but not necessarily so in the Beaumont report, and the Bystander said he lived at Sour Lake while Houston dispatches called him "of Houston."

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Sour Lake, Texas
bases: Notices ordered all Black people out of Sour Lake, a mob of about 500 raided the Black camps with gunfire, employers were told to discharge Black workers, and 50 to 200 people were reported driven out (A4, A5, A18, A23).

The AP Sour Lake dispatch (A4), the Houston Post special (A7), an independent Houston dispatch to the New York Sun (A5) and a New Orleans dispatch (A23) all report the notices and the driving out of Black residents.

accounts.gist: Thompson fatally wounded by a negro; notices in 25-30 places; over fifty left; restaurant guarded; night raid by 500 men with about 100 shots; Mexican beaten; proprietors warned.

accounts.label: Houston Post special from Sour Lake
accounts.gist: Same core, adding the hour, Thompson in a Beaumont hospital, notices in 25 or 35 places, and that an effort would be made to protect the negroes at the guarded restaurant.

accounts.label: Houston dispatch to the New York Sun
accounts.gist: Black refugees reaching Houston said an armed mob drove them out; a 'negro tramp' shot Thompson; 'some person' posted notices and about 100 left; much shooting in the oil field.

accounts.label: Beaumont special to the San Antonio Daily Light
accounts.gist: W. D. Thompson shot through the breast at Nome by a negro tramp; wound not necessarily fatal.

accounts.label: Houston follow-up, July 10
accounts.gist: Trouble quieted; workers promised protection against the 'hoodlum element'; Mexican to recover; a beaten Black man missing.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch, July 11 (white citizens' version)
accounts.gist: The 'better class' of whites stopped the mob from threatening law-abiding negroes; about 200, 'including the entire criminal and dangerous element,' were driven out.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP dispatch as news, many printing the notice's slur ('Notice to "Niggers."' in the Deseret Evening News; the Indianapolis Journal's subhead).
Southern headlines forecast 'Race War' and called the shooting 'Murder' though Thompson was not reported dead.
The New York Sun's 'Stood Up for the Negroes' praised the 'better class' of whites while calling those expelled the 'criminal and dangerous element'.
Northern headlines and digests named the attack: 'Shooting Negroes in Texas', 'Drive Negroes From Oil Fields', 'Raiding Negroes in Texas'.
The Iowa State Bystander ran the AP text under 'Drive Negroes From Town / Murder of Brakeman ... Starts War' with no comment.

conflicts.note: Counts were made at different times; the 200 figure comes from a later New Orleans dispatch that also characterizes those expelled.
The Beaumont special, from the city where he was hospitalized, is the earliest report; no report of his death or recovery was found.
The Lamar Register's condensed reprint is the outlier, likely an error.
The later report (July 10) supersedes the first.
The Kennebec Journal's brief misplaced the expulsion.
